title: POC Variant Scheduling and Prompt Pipeline Playbook
content:
Context and goal:

This note captures the playbook we used during a recent mid-stage POC with a retail search customer. Primary goal: find a model+serving configuration that meets 95th-percentile latency <= 250ms for single-turn product-summarization calls, while keeping per-1M-token hosted cost under $X (customer target). Secondary goals: maintain answer quality above baseline F1/ROUGE thresholds, and produce deterministic fallbacks when the primary model fails sampling/regression tests.

Key constraints:
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 250ms (strict for interactive UI)
- Throughput target: 150 reqs/min sustained, 400 reqs/min burstable
- Sensitive fields: customer forbids sending raw PII to third-party models; private-deployment or dedicated pool required for any full-context traces
- Allowed model families: open-weights (e.g., Llama-family variants), and selected vetted weights on Redwood catalog (customer legal review pending)
- HW: target deployment on A100s for dedicated, with a guarded fallback to lower-cost T4-like nodes for non-critical routes

Approach summary (high level):
1) Multi-variant routing. Keep two primary model classes live: a quality-first float16 variant (base model) and a cost-first 4-bit/GPTQ variant. Use policy-based routing by request class: interactive UI => route to float16 when within latency budget; otherwise route to 4-bit.
2) Activation thresholds. Compute an "activation score" per request based on prompt length, expected output length, and precedence (e.g., admin vs consumer). For low-score requests, always use quantized variant. For high-score (rich context), try float16 then fallback to quantized variant only on capacity/timeouts.
3) Prefix & KV caching. Aggressively cache common product prefix tokens and static metadata to reduce repeated decode cost. Cache keys are content digest + model-variant-id + prompt-template-id.
4) Prompt pipeline decomposition. Break heavy requests into: retrieval -> short context synthesis -> single-shot summarization. Use a small embedding-based reranker and a compact conditional prompt generator to keep the expensive model input length small.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Models: rwi-70B-f16 (baseline), rwi-70B-gptq-4 (4-bit), owl-13B-f16 (cheap float), owl-13B-8bit (INT8 experiment), distilled-7B-4bit (edge candidate)
- Quant methods: GPTQ post-hoc 4-bit, AWQ 4/8 mix, int8 dynamic-range fallback
- Batching strategies: micro-batch size 1 (low latency), adaptive burst batching (accumulate for up to 10ms), and conservative batching for background routes
- Caching: no-cache, prefix-cache (static prod metadata), KV-cache per user-session (30s TTL)
- Routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, hybrid (priority + token-budget checks)
- Guardrails: automatic quality regression check using a lightweight eval on a holdout prompt set (30 prompts) per deployment change

Metrics captured per cell: p50/p95 latency, tokens/response, effective tokens billed, per-1M-token cost estimate, QA-f1, rouge-L, regression-fail-count, fallback-rate (requests that migrated to cheaper/alternative model due to capacity or timeouts).

Key lessons and surprising results:
- 4-bit GPTQ variants reduced token compute by ~3.8x in practice but introduced occasional hallucination spikes for edge-case prompts (long, multi-entity lists). We observed a 6% drop in rouge-L on product-attribute heavy test slices.
- Mixed precision (float16 primary with int8 decode path) gave the best tradeoff for throughput on A100: p95 stayed under budget while avg cost fell ~25% compared to pure float16 for the same request mix.
- Aggressive prefix caching (server-side) reduced average input tokens by 18% and dropped p95 by ~60ms. The cache TTL of 30s hit the sweet spot for UI flows.
- Adaptive micro-batching (10ms accumulation) improved GPU utilization for burst windows but introduced tail-latency outliers for single-actor interactive flows. Best to enable only on background or timeout-insensitive endpoints.

Prompt/pipeline tuning notes (practical):
- Synthesize short context: create an intermediate prompt template that converts raw retrieval hits into a 1–3 sentence context summary. This reduced cold-input length and improved quantized-model robustness.
- Token budget guard: instrument prompt builder to ensure post-context prompt <= 1024 tokens for quantized variants, otherwise escalate to float16 only if latency headroom exists.
- Negative examples: add 6–8 short negative examples to training set for product lists to reduce hallucinations in quantized run. These are short, targeted instructions that say "do not invent attributes not in the context".
- Temperature tuning: lower temperature (0.0–0.2) on quantized variants to reduce variance; keep float16 at 0.7 for creative summarization lanes.

Failure/recovery patterns and runbook items:
- Timeout fallback: if quantized inference exceeds 350ms, route request to float16 once (if capacity allows) or serve a cached/abbreviated response with transparent UI note.
- Quality regression detection: schedule nightly mini-eval (50 prompts capturing edge cases) and fail rollout if >3 regressions vs baseline. Rollback policy is automatic to the last known-good model-variant with notification to on-call SE.
- Metric drift alarms: set alerts on sudden spike in fallback-rate (>5% over baseline) and on RUOK tests failing (synthetic prompt set).

Quick wins to propose for next customer demo:
- Enable prefix caching for top-10 product templates (fast, low-risk, measurable latency wins).
- Deploy rwi-70B-f16 + rwi-70B-gptq-4 with hybrid routing and show cost comparison panel in the dashboard (p50/p95 + cost/1M tokens).
- Add 30 curated negative prompt examples aimed at list hallucinations; re-run the quant calibration sweep.

Proposed timeline for an 8-week POC:
- Week 0: kickoff, data handoff (catalog of product pages, retrieval endpoints), and baseline metric collection
- Week 1–2: model variant builds (GPTQ + AWQ experiments), prefix cache prototype, prompt pipeline refactor into synth-step
- Week 3–4: integration into dedicated pool, routing policy stub, run first QA sweep and cost simulation
- Week 5: user-simulated load test and latency tuning, enable adaptive caching strategies
- Week 6: catalogue edge-case prompt evaluation, finalize rollout & rollback policies, stakeholder demo prep
- Week 7–8: final tuning, internal runbook handover, customer demo and next-step commercial proposal

Open questions and decisions needed from customer:
- Acceptable deterministic fallback messaging in UI when we shorten output due to latency?
- Is deployment into Redwood Dedicated enough for compliance, or do they require Private (VPC/on-prem)?
- Will they allow server-side caching of partial product metadata (PII risk assessment)?

Next actions for our team (short list):
- Aisha: finalize GPTQ build scripts and share run commands in the repo (github link in artifacts).
- Marco: instrument prompt-builder with token-budget enforcement and a weak-mode (warn-only) flag for initial rollout.
- Dana: prototype prefix-cache middleware with per-key TTL configurability and telemetry hooks.
- Priya: assemble the 30-point mini-eval set that targets hallucination-prone slices (lists, rare attributes, long context)

Notes for archive: store raw mini-eval JSON, tokenized baselines, and GPU perf traces under JIRA-POC-78 in the artifacts bucket. Keep model artifacts locked during legal review.

Appendix: sample prompt templates (short)
- Retrieval->synth template:
  "Given these product bullet points, summarize the most important 3 features in 1-2 sentences focused on customer benefit. Do not invent details. Context: {{retrieval_snippet}}"
- Summarization final step:
  "Using the context above, write a short product blurb (max 60 words) suitable for web listing. Be concise and factual. If missing key specs, say 'Specs limited'."

End of playbook note.
